## Entropy (statistical thermodynamics) - Wikipedia
Boltzmann's entropy describes the system when all the accessible microstates are equally likely. It is the configuration corresponding to the maximum of entropy at equilibrium. The randomness or disorder is maximal, and so is the lack of distinction (or information) of each microstate. Entropy is a thermodynamic property just like pressure, volume, or temperature. Therefore, it connects the microscopic and the macroscopic world view. [...] Ludwig Boltzmann defined entropy as a measure of the number of possible microscopic states (microstates) of a system in thermodynamic equilibrium, consistent with its macroscopic thermodynamic properties, which constitute the macrostate of the system. The easily measurable parameters volume, pressure, and temperature of the gas describe its macroscopic condition (state).

plan.title: Entropy: Why Heat Never Flows Backward
plan.description: Entropy counts the ways a system can be arranged, and the second law says it never decreases on its own. This explains why ice melts, heat flows from hot to cold, and time seems to run one way.

beats.narration: A hot coffee always cools down. A cold room never makes it hot again. Why does heat only travel one way?
The answer is a quantity called entropy. Many people call it disorder, but that word hides the real idea.
Picture a messy desk and a tidy desk. There are countless ways to be messy, but very few ways to be tidy.
Physicists call each exact arrangement of molecules a microstate. The overall look, like pressure and temperature, is the macrostate.
Ludwig Boltzmann turned this into an equation. Entropy equals a constant, k, times the natural log of W, the number of microstates.

steps.note: W is the number of microstates

beats.narration: More microstates means more entropy. A higher temperature, more molecules, or a larger volume all give a system more ways to arrange itself.
Open a bottle of perfume and the scent spreads across the room. Spread-out molecules have vastly more arrangements than packed ones.
The second law says total entropy in a spontaneous process either increases or stays constant. It never decreases.

props.definition: In any spontaneous process, total entropy increases or stays constant. It never decreases.

beats.narration: For heat, the change in entropy is the heat transferred, Q, divided by the temperature, T.
Heat leaving a hot object lowers its entropy a little. The same heat entering a colder object raises entropy more. Overall, entropy goes up.
That is why heat flows from hot to cold, and never the reverse by itself. The reverse would lower total entropy.
Melting ice shows it. Heat flows in, and the rigid crystal becomes free-moving liquid with many more microstates.
Entropy can fall in one place if it rises more elsewhere. A fridge cools food, but its heat raises entropy in the room.
So entropy is not mess. It is the count of ways things can be, and nature drifts toward the most likely arrangement.

props.text: Heat flows downhill because there are more ways to be spread out.

accuracy.reason: Core claims match the notes: Boltzmann S=k ln W, second law, ΔS=Q/T, and the fridge example. Small imprecision: the 'higher temperature, more molecules, larger volume' list is stated as a rule, and the hot-to-cold explanation skips the point that the temperatures are treated as roughly constant.

coverage.reason: Covers microstates, the second law, heat flow and melting ice, and corrects the 'disorder' idea. It omits the arrow of time, why life doesn't violate the second law, and a shuffled-deck example, and it spends a lot of time on formulas.

structure.reason: The order is clear: hook, microstates, equation, second law, examples, takeaway. Beat 6 (what raises entropy) sits awkwardly before the perfume example, and the formula-heavy middle makes the pacing dense.

hook_ending.reason: The coffee question is a decent hook. The ending restates the thesis ('nature drifts toward the most likely arrangement') rather than giving a vivid closing image.

tone.reason: Conversational and clear for beginners, but the equations and the natural-log mention lean technical for a 2-minute explainer.

visuals.reason: Good variety of clips, diagrams, equations and a versus card, and each matches its narration. The two equation scenes and several text-heavy scenes are somewhat dry, and the beat 10 diagram edge is odd.

originality.reason: The messy desk, perfume, ice and fridge examples are standard textbook fare. The 'disorder hides the real idea' reframing is good but common.

instructions.reason: English, roughly the right length, and it explains entropy. It misses some of the expected items (arrow of time, life).

language.reason: Fluent, with short clear sentences. 'Heat flows downhill because there are more ways to be spread out' is slightly loose.

judge.summary: A clear, accurate, well-ordered explainer that reframes entropy as counting microstates, but it is equation-heavy and leans on stock examples. It skips the arrow of time and life, and it ends on a plain summary.
